In the construction of Lebesgue integration on a general unsigned measure space (X,M,μ) {(X,\mathfrak{M},\mu)}(X,M,μ), the class of L1 {L^{1}}L1-integrable functions is readly built into the integration theory, namely, the extended-real-valued measurable functions f:X→[−∞,+∞] {f:X\rightarrow[-\infty,+\infty]}f:X→[−∞,+∞] satisfying the absolute integrable condition

∫X∣f∣dμ<∞.\displaystyle \int_{X}|f|d\mu<\infty.∫X​∣f∣dμ<∞.

A notable feature of Lebesgue integration is that it doen't "count'' the behavior of a function on a null set. Indeed, recall that we have adopted the convention that

+∞⋅0=−∞⋅0=0\displaystyle +\infty\cdot0=-\infty\cdot0=0+∞⋅0=−∞⋅0=0

which we have to use when definining the integral for simple functions. This makes the multiplilcation to be upward continuous, in the sense that if xn≥0↗x {x_{n}\geq0\nearrow x}xn​≥0↗x and yn≥0↗y {y_{n}\geq0\nearrow y}yn​≥0↗y, then xnyn≥0↗xy {x_{n}y_{n}\geq0\nearrow xy}xn​yn​≥0↗xy. We don't have this general convergence for monotonely decreasing ones. Ultimately, it leads to approximating integrals from below rather than above, as prominently shown by monotone convergence theorem. Thus we see that the measurable function can behave arbitrarily on an unknown null set, where the integral (if exists) still remains unchanged. It is now that we take a step forward to consider "functions'' that are only defined almost everywhere, abbr. a.e., i.e. the equivalent classes modulo a.e. equality, with the caution that we now lost the ability to evaluate the equivalent class [f] {[f]}[f] at a specific point x∈X {x\in X}x∈X. However it is almost harmless to think of these equivalent classes as functions in practice. We deonte by L1(μ) {L^{1}(\mu)}L1(μ), or simply L1, {L^{1},}L1, the space of all equivalent classes of functions that are absolutely integrable on the measure space (X,M,μ) {(X,\mathfrak{M},\mu)}(X,M,μ). And the context should be clear where we are using functions or equivalent classes. As an immediate consequence of L1 {L^{1}}L1-integrability, we have ∣f∣<∞ {|f|<\infty}∣f∣<∞ a.e. This is sometimes useful for developing a.e. convergence of certain integrands.
